title: Hannah Aldridge, Mike Brewer & Matthew Cavanagh, "Home economics: How to put England's broken housing taxes on firmer foundations", Resolution Foundation briefing note, 24 September 2026 (doi 10.63492/kpyf844)

verdict: NEW research/resolution-foundation-home-economics.md (a research page for a Tier 1 source: independent research institute, CC-BY-NC-ND licensed, authors Aldridge/Brewer/Cavanagh; Mike Brewer a Tier 1 academic economist per the queue note, whose standing was not independently re-checked here). Frame as a PROPERTY-VALUE proportional tax, not an LVT; the report discusses LVT explicitly and declines it (Box 1, p.14). ENRICH (short attributed paragraph + See Also, not restatement): (1) people/andy-burnham.md - the competing-proposals section beside the Fairer Share 0.48% paragraph; the report never names Burnham (it says 'a new Prime Minister who has vowed to close regional gaps', p.3, and 'the Prime Minister's central ambition of addressing regional inequality', p.37), so tie to him only via that wording and the Fairer Share release, not as an endorsement; (2) places/united-kingdom.md - one sentence in the 2026 debate paragraph on the OECD-highest property-tax share (3.7% of GDP in 2023 vs OECD average 2%, p.7), which bears directly on the 'is land undertaxed' passage there (the page cites ~2.8% recurrent / ~3.7% including stamp duties); (3) research/muellbauer-property-tax-reform-england.md - See Also line and a sentence in 'Relation to the Georgist Case' making it five differently designed reforms (the page currently says 'four'): RF is a whole-stock, single-rate replacement of council tax AND main-rate stamp duty, whereas Muellbauer is a top-slice surcharge with tapered SDLT cut. Also add See Also both ways with research/tpa-what-would-lvt-do.md (RF cites Neidle for stamp-duty credit schemes, fn37 p.33; both use a 3% discount-rate-style capitalisation and deferral) and research/mirrlees-review.md (RF states its ideal is 'akin to the approach proposed by the Mirrlees Review', p.4, fn35 p.33), and ahmadi-ghenis-uk-council-tax-lvt-microsimulation.md (LVT-based 0.79% vs RF 0.66-0.7% property-value base: useful contrast). Do NOT present as support for LVT: it argues the opposite on base, though it grants the 'very strong theoretical case' for an LVT (p.14). New page needs >=2 inbound links (Burnham, UK, Muellbauer pages will supply them). Suggested page frame: 'the most authoritative current UK reform proposal on a property-value base; a Georgist reader should read it as a Tier 1 statement of what a mainstream, non-LVT reform looks like and why it stops short of land'.
claim_grade: A for what the report says and proposes (Tier 1 source per EDITORIAL 4c: independent research institute, published full text read). B for its modelled figures - 2030-31 projections from the authors' own microsimulation (HBAI/FRS 2024-25 + IPPR tax-benefit model + imputed property values), with stated assumptions (90/10 landlord/tenant incidence; stamp duty annualised over 20 years; 3% capitalisation discount rate; OBR 2017 stamp-duty semi-elasticities); not independently replicated. The '100,000 purchases' figure is a press-release rounding, not a report figure - grade it C until reconciled (see below).
content_summary: PROPOSAL (pp.3-6, 14-17). Replace Council Tax (England) and the main rates of residential Stamp Duty with one annual proportional property tax at a flat 0.7% of current property value (capital value, incl. land and buildings). Rate derivation (p.16-17): England is set to raise GBP59bn of Council Tax net of discounts/rebates (incl. High Value Council Tax Surcharge) plus GBP15bn main-rate Stamp Duty in 2030-31 = GBP74bn to replace (OBR March 2026 forecast, England share estimated by RF, fn18); housing stock 2030-31 estimated GBP10.9tn after capitalisation effects (fn19); 0.66% is 'approximately revenue neutral', slightly more needed for means-tested rebates; 'alongside surcharges on dwellings that are not someone's main home raising at least GBP3bn', 0.7% is revenue-neutral after rebates, ignoring deferrals (which are delayed not lost). NOTE the headline 0.7% therefore assumes >=GBP3bn from separate second-home/empty-home surcharges (fn20, drawing on Fairer Share's estimates of GBP2.4bn 2019-20 and GBP4.5bn for foreign-owned/empty/second homes). fn21: 'a degree of consensus among commentators that a cost-neutral tax rate would fall between 0.6 per cent and 0.7 per cent'; RF sits at the top because of a lower stock valuation (MHCLG Market Value Survey) and because it targets 2030-31; Prosperity 2030 (UCL IGP, Percy, July 2026) proposes 1.0% (social housing exempt, extra revenue for services); also cites M Dent (Property Tax Lab) and B Ansell (IPPR, Aug 2026). WHO PAYS: the occupier, as with Council Tax (fn15 p.15: chosen to limit transition difficulty of shifting legal incidence from tenants to landlords and avoid non-compliance). Economic incidence: RF assumes 90% of any change in the recurrent tax falls on landlords (via rents) and 10% on tenants (Box 3, p.18; cites England 2016, Oates & Fischel 2016, IFS Adam et al 2020). REBATES/DEFERRAL (Box 2, pp.15-16): a Council-Tax-Benefit-style national means-tested rebate that also counts home equity; owner-occupiers with equity below 35% get the rebate; those with more equity get deferral to a lump sum at sale (35% threshold chosen so 50 years of deferral cannot produce negative equity; cliff-edge for mortgagors discussed fn17); the single-person 25% discount is abolished; a deferral scheme needs design work and has a history of low take-up internationally (p.36, cites Muellbauer 2023 OECD chapter). LOCAL: a national rate set for revenue neutrality with councils able to vary it (p.31); grants to local government would need redistributing toward councils that currently over-collect - RF explicitly does not set out how (pp.30-31). TRANSITION (pp.5-6, 33-37): first step is a fresh valuation database, launched 'at the first opportunity, which is... the upcoming Autumn Budget', at least two years' work (p.5, 35); freeze Stamp Duty rates for the rest of this Parliament and commit that stamp duty paid in the transition counts as a credit against future property tax bills, usable for a time-limited 2-5 years and only where a homeowner's annual charge rises (pp.5-6, 33-34); phase bills in over four years for owners (year 1 = 3/4 old + 1/4 new, fully implemented by year 4; p.34); for private renters apply the new bill when the tenant moves or after five years, whichever is sooner (p.35); unfreeze and index Local Housing Allowance (residual cost ~GBP50m in 2030-31, p.41) and announce a targeted Starter Deposit Scheme equity loan (p.36); commit to no Stamp Duty rate cuts until a commission reports. COMMISSION (p.37, p.6): 'launch a commission into the residential property tax system, to examine the winners and losers from the current system, how it could be improved and how the transition could be dealt with' - covering local and regional devolution, housebuilding and social-care funding (p.37). DIAGNOSIS (pp.3, 7-13): UK raises 3.7% of GDP in property taxes (2023) vs OECD average 2% (OECD Global Revenue Statistics); Council Tax 1.7% -> 1.9% of GDP and Stamp Duty 0.6% -> 0.8% of GDP 2025-26 to 2030-31 (p.8); HVCTS raises <GBP0.5bn a year (p.8); prices since Jan 1995 up 7.3x in Inner London, 6.0x East of England, 4.2x North East (p.11); a property at the bottom of the top band in Richmond-upon-Thames is worth 15x one at the top of the bottom band in Hull but its Council Tax bill is only just over double; Hull's resident pays over GBP1,800 a year more than at Richmond's effective rate (p.11, fn10); median effective rate 1.5% for a GBP100k home vs 0.6% for a GBP1m home by 2030-31 (p.10); for a GBP200k home the interquartile range of effective rates is 0.5-1.2% (p.10); 2024-25 tax as share of housing value: North East 0.8% vs London 0.4% (p.12). DISTRIBUTION (pp.3-4, 12, 19-23, 31-33; comparisons are current system vs a uniform proportional tax, England 2030-31): London underpaid GBP3.1bn in 2024-25 relative to a uniform rate; rest of England would pay GBP12.3bn less if taxed at London's rate (pp.3, 12); 61% of households overpay (avg GBP430/yr), 36% underpay (avg GBP680/yr), 3% pay about the same (p.19); 68% see a change of >=GBP250 either way (p.23); North East: 85% overpay, avg GBP710/yr; London: 80% underpay, avg GBP950/yr; outside London 68% overpay, and in all regions outside London over half overpay (p.20); income: 63% of households below the 80th percentile lose from the current system, 56% of the top 5% underpay (pp.20-21); winners and losers spread across the income distribution - e.g. in the second vigintile 48% overpay by >=GBP250 and 25% underpay by >=GBP250 (p.21); multi-adult households outside London: 61% overpay by >=GBP250; single-adult households outside London: 55% gain, 38% lose; single adults in London: 68% underpay by >=GBP250, 20% still overpay (p.22); under the reform about a quarter (25%) of households at the very bottom of the income distribution would still pay >=GBP250 more even with rebates (p.4); the reform is 'more progressive (with respect to household income)': bottom half pay slightly less, top pay much more (Fig 13, p.32). No tenure table beyond the private-rented incidence assumption; no value-band table beyond Fig 3 (p.10); NO council-level figures: the model uses regional (not local-authority) average tax bases and the report says this may understate both large winners and losers (Annex 2, p.40); the only local-authority comparison is the Hull/Richmond illustration (p.11). PRICE EFFECTS (pp.29-30, Fig 12, chart values read off image, approximate): median property value change with council tax replaced and stamp duty kept / with both replaced - North East about +12.5% / +13.7%; North West +7.5% / +8.8%; West Midlands +4% / +5.7%; Yorkshire & Humber +5.6% / +7%; South West +0.4% / +3.3%; East Midlands +2.3% / +4.3%; South East -1.6% / +1.8%; East of England -1.4% / +1.6%; London -8% / -4%. Capitalisation modelled at a 3% discount rate with full pass-through (p.40). STAMP DUTY (pp.24-29, 41-42): ~800,000 liable transactions in 2030-31; abolishing the main rate would add ~92,000 house moves, an 11% increase (p.24; OBR 2017 semi-elasticities; 'the scale of this response is difficult to predict'; fn25 notes other research finds larger responses, Hilber & Lyytikainen 2017); by band (Fig 9): baseline 238k/356k/175k/32k/8k under GBP250k/250-500k/500k-1m/1-2m/over 2m, additional 12k/39k/26k/12k/3k (sums to 92k; labels taken from the figure text layer in order); GDP +0.04% central (range +0.02% to +0.11%) from labour mobility after 10 years of extra moves (Fig 10, p.25); deadweight loss of main-rate stamp duty: simple Harberger triangle 12% of revenue (lower bound), literature ~60% (Australian CGE) to ~120% (Finland 130%; Toronto 111%) (Fig 11, pp.27-28, 42); it also mentions Chang et al. (2025) modelling +3.38% GDP from replacing stamp duties with a broad annual land tax in Australia, described as highly uncertain (p.42); abolishing stamp duty alone would raise prices and give windfalls to current owners (p.29). LAND VERSUS PROPERTY VALUE (Box 1, pp.13-15; Box 2 not relevant). Base choice: the 'theoretical ideal' is a proportional tax on the rental value of housing services consumed, treated as a consumption tax; because of owner-occupation, use capital value of the property for valuation, public understanding and legitimacy (p.14). The report's own words on LVT: 'What of a land value tax (LVT)? There is a very strong theoretical case for such a tax: land is in fixed supply and its value is not changed by human effort, so taxing it would not disincentivise any activity that we would value. On the other hand, bringing the building into the tax base can disincentivise things we would like to see, such as construction or improvements.' It then follows the Mirrlees Review that, since one would like to tax both land and land+property, 'applying one rate is preferable for practical reasons', and adds that 'The tax base for an LVT would be even more geographically concentrated than for a proportional property tax: land makes up a larger share of a property's value where property values are higher, so the changes would be even more extreme and the transition harder' (p.14). So: a practical/transition argument for the property base, plus a legitimacy argument; it does NOT dispute the efficiency case for land, does not cite Neidle's or PolicyEngine's LVT models for that point, and does not discuss land valuation methods. Its footnotes cite Neidle (Tax Policy Associates, July 2026) only for credit schemes (fn37) and Chang et al. for the Australian annual land tax result (fn53). Its deadweight/behaviour argument for recurrent taxes: quotes OECD 'recurrent taxes on immovable property are considered one of the most economically efficient forms of taxation' (pp.14-15). Also floats extra surcharges on second homes and empty properties (fn20). THE '100,000 PURCHASES' CLAIM. It is NOT in the report. The RF press release (24 Sept 2026) says: 'The authors add that Stamp Duty also prevents around 100,000 house purchases every year.' The corresponding report figure is ~92,000 additional house moves (an 11% rise on ~800,000 liable transactions) in 2030-31 if the main rate were abolished (p.24, Fig 9) - a model estimate using OBR 2017 elasticities, not an observed count; trade press repeats the 100,000 wording. Cite the report's 92,000 and label the 100,000 as the press release's rounding. COMPARISONS. Fairer Share: not compared with a rate. Named only as one example of prior proportional-property-tax advocacy (fn35 p.33, citing Dixon et al, The Proportional Property Tax Manifesto, Oct 2021) and as the source for second/empty/foreign-owned home surcharge revenue estimates (fn20); the report never mentions 0.48%, the 0.96% double rate, Burnham or the 25 Sept Fairer Share release. Read side by side, RF's 0.66-0.7% is well above Fairer Share's 0.48%; RF says commentators converge on 0.6-0.7% (fn21), so the wiki should present the two rates as different designs by different bodies without asserting which is 'right' or that RF criticises Fairer Share (it does not). Muellbauer: thanked in the acknowledgements for 'useful conversations and suggestions' (p.2); cited for property tax reform options (Housing, Debt and the Economy, NIER 2018; 'Land, Housing and the British Economy: background paper', INET Oxford Working Paper 2025-25, February 2026; fn35 p.33) and for deferral design (his 2023 OECD chapter 'Why we need a green land value tax and how to design it', fn42 p.36). The report does not discuss his HVCTS/PHVCTS surcharge design, the Sept 2026 INET paper 2026-24, or the taper formula. Similarities: joint council-tax/stamp-duty reform, immediate stamp-duty stability, credit for recent stamp duty paid, deferral for asset-rich, need for revaluation. Differences: whole-stock 0.7% replacement vs a top-slice 0.5%/1% surcharge above GBP1.5m; RF sequences valuation first, then a four-year phase-in. Also cites the CenTax 'Tax Reforms for Growth' (Nov 2025), IFS 'Revaluation and reform' (Adam et al 2020), IPPR (Nanda 2021; Ansell Aug 2026), UCL IGP Prosperity 2030 (Percy July 2026) as fellow proponents.

uncertainties: 1) The '100,000 purchases prevented' figure appears only in the press release and trade press; the report's own number is 92,000 additional moves (11%) in 2030-31, a modelled estimate the authors call 'difficult to predict'. 2) The 0.7% is neutral only with >=GBP3bn from separate second-home/empty-home surcharges; the base 0.66% (+ rebates) is the no-surcharge figure; the report does not publish a rate excluding the surcharges precisely. 3) Winner/loser results compare the current system against a hypothetical uniform proportional tax in 2030-31, with stamp duty annualised over 20 years and 90% landlord incidence - they are not a forecast of gains from the transition path (phasing is not modelled in the tables). 4) Regional, not council-level, results; the model probably understates extremes (p.40). 5) Figure 12 values above are eyeballed from the chart (approximate, +/- ~0.5 point); Fig 9 labels were matched by order from the text layer but sum correctly (92k additional, ~809k baseline). 6) The Fairer Share 0.48% vs RF 0.66-0.7% gap is not explained by the report; do not attribute an explanation. 7) RF does not discuss valuation methods, mass appraisal, or how a land-only value would be separated - so it is silent on the 'land cannot be assessed' objection. 8) Burnham is never named; the ENRICH on his page should be about the policy debate, not his position. 9) The report is a briefing note (43 pp incl. annexes), not peer-reviewed; the wiki has a Tier 1 gloss on RF as an independent research institute (charity 1114839) - if T1 doubts RF's tier, the fallback is Tier 2 'proponent' framing, but the rubric (independent institute, published methodology, named economists) supports Tier 1. 10) Mike Brewer's individual tier was taken from the queue note; the RF page lists him as an author, but his academic record was not re-checked in this pass. 11) CC BY-NC-ND licence: short attributed quotes (<=50 words) only; do not reproduce figures wholesale.
